While the upper crown appears seasonally normal, the root system, structural root plate, and critical root zone show long-standing impacts. trees.comments: This pine is fully dead. The crown contains no live foliage, with complete needle browning and branch desiccation throughout the canopy. Structural integrity is compromised due to prolonged standing mortality, making the tree an elevated failure risk.

This tree is dead, retaining leaves far beyond the normal abscission period and exhibiting no live buds. Ambrosia beetle frass is visible at the base, indicating colonization of dead or dying wood and confirming vascular system collapse. Bark is loose and sounding confirms internal decay.

A prominent vertical decay column is present along the main stem, with exposed inner wood and bark separation indicating an active and advancing decay process. Structural stability is reduced as decay progresses upward within the trunk.

The tree has a co-dominant structure with a previously failed leader, leaving a major decayed stub with exposed heartwood. Compartmentalization around the wound is incomplete, leaving an open pathway for decay to extend downward into the parent stem and a critical union. The remaining canopy shows asymmetrical loading and chronic structural imbalance.

The tree exhibits a basal wound with exposed heartwood and developing decay. A ram’s-horn shaped wound at the trunk flare has not closed and continues to deteriorate. The canopy is asymmetrical and shows signs of chronic stress, suggesting reduced structural capacity.
Tree is fully dead, with complete canopy decline and no visible live buds or live cambial tissue. Branch structure is brittle and desiccated.

The tree appears dead, retaining desiccated leaves and showing full canopy collapse. Significant ambrosia beetle frass is present at the trunk base and within multiple bark fissures, indicating sustained attack on dead wood. Combined with crown condition, the evidence confirms total tree failure.

The trunk exhibits a pronounced dogleg bend with abnormal swelling at the bend point, suggesting internal weakness or decay. The geometry creates an elevated bending moment at the defect site. Further up the leader is a old branch site with decay extending to the main stem.

A significant vertical cavity is present at the site of a former co-dominant union. The cavity exposes decayed inner wood and reveals incomplete compartmentalization around the failure site. This configuration leaves the tree structurally compromised with limited remaining cross-sectional strength.

A large structural cavity exists where the main stem sweeps horizontally, located directly on the compression side of the bend. The exposed decayed heartwood at this point substantially weakens the load-bearing portion of the stem. The defect extends upward into the union, reducing structural integrity throughout the primary scaffold.

The tree shows severe canopy thinning and limited live foliage concentrated only in the uppermost branches, indicating a very low live crown ratio. Basal irregularities and signs of long-term stress are present, and the overall canopy vigor suggests irreversible decline consistent with advanced physiological failure.

The lower stem exhibits vertical bark loss and exposed cambial tissue consistent with deer antler rubbing. The wound is elongated and extends into the lower trunk, compromising the tree’s vascular continuity and increasing vulnerability to decay fungi.

Tree 13 has two basal cavities with interior hollowing, each with a different-sized opening. The tree also has a primary codominant union with included bark, likely formed after an older breakage or top-out event. Further up the trunk, a leader appears to have broken in the past, and a subordinate branch/leader has taken over, creating a twisted growth pattern with poor taper at a stair-step bend. The upper portion of the canopy leans toward the right-of-way. This tree also has a deformed structural root plate, similar to that of Tree 14.

This tree has a symmetrical codominant leader structure with included bark. One wound site shows evidence of an older breakage or top-out event, and a decayed leader remnant is visible at that location. This defect is notable because it lies just below the co-dominant union. The tree also shares a deformed structural root plate with Tree 13, as both trees are growing into each other at the base, reducing normal root plate development.

The pine has a dead leader stub at the co-dominant union displaying exposed decayed heartwood. The decay extends into the union area, significantly weakening structural continuity between the main stems. Multiple branch failures and thin canopy distribution indicate declining vigor and compromised mechanical stability.
